Motivation
"How can we architect agent memory as a dynamic cognitive faculty, capable of fluid, reconstructive processes that interweave seamlessly with reasoning?"
Fig. 1 — Parametric memory modifies weights via SFT/GRPO/DPO → catastrophic forgetting. Retrieval-based appends context once at task start. MemGen generates latent vectors Mt woven into the hidden-state stream during reasoning. Core LLM πθ always frozen.
Failure modes of prior paradigms & MemGen advantages
Prior paradigms
Parametric: catastrophic forgetting, erodes general knowledge
Retrieval: rigid one-time context append at task start
Retrieval: efficacy tethered to backbone capacity
Prior latent: still similarity-based retrieval, invasive param updates
MemGen advantages
Generative reconstruction — not retrieval
Core πθ frozen — no forgetting by design
Token-level dynamic memory insertion
Optimization-agnostic: SFT or GRPO
Compatible with external retrieval DBs
MemGen architecture
Fig. 2 — Trigger T reads Ht,<j at each delimiter and samples INVOKE/SKIP. On INVOKE, Weaver W synthesizes Mt and prepends it to the hidden-state sequence. Reasoner πθ resumes conditioned on enriched context. Both T and W are LoRA adapters on the frozen πθ.
Core equations
pj = σ(𝚫trigger(ht,1, … ,ht,j−1))
Invocation probability at delimiter token j;  dj ∼ Bernoulli(pj) ∈ {INVOKE, SKIP}
Mt := 𝐎weaver(Ht,<j) ∈ ℝK × d
Latent memory matrix;  K ∈ {2, 4, 8};  selective reconstruction, not retrieval
zt,j ∼ πθ( · |st,zt,<j,Mt)
Next token sampled from frozen reasoner conditioned on enriched hidden-state context
Training pipeline — two sequential stages
Stage 1 — Train Wweaver
Trigger fixed (random inserter). Gradients → only LoRA θ′. Core πθ untouched.
SFT: −𝔼[log πθ(zt,j* | st,zt,<j*,Mt)]
GRPO: Group-relative advantage reward with KL penalty on θ′
Stage 2 — Train Ttrigger
Weaver frozen. RL objective:
max 𝔼[R(τ) − λ∑max(0, d̃j − p̄)]
p̄ = mean activation of high-reward trajectories. Sparsity-adaptive penalty discourages over-invocation while preserving critical memory calls.

MemGen consistently advances all 9 benchmarks across both backbones. Retrieval-based methods collapse on reasoning tasks (ExpeL GPQA: 8.12% on Qwen2.5-1.5B, below vanilla 11.62%). MemGen is the only system that advances all domains simultaneously.
RQ3 — Continual learning: mitigates catastrophic forgetting (Table 5)
Sequential training on Qwen2.5-1.5B: AQuA → GPQA → GSM8K → KodCode. Performance on earlier tasks after final KodCode stage:
MethodAQuAGPQAGSM8KKodCode
SFT28.612.5324.1454.10
ExpeL27.146.2331.4448.35
MemGen SFT ★40.3420.0953.7252.95
SFT catastrophically forgets: GPQA drops to 2.53% after KodCode training. MemGen preserves AQuA at 40.34% and GPQA at 20.09%.

Why? Experience updates only Wweaver’s LoRA θ′. Core πθ never modified → general capabilities structurally preserved.
RQ2 — Cross-domain generalisation (Fig. 3 & Fig. 4)
Fig. 3 — Train on one dataset, evaluate on four. SFT and MemoryBank degrade out-of-domain (FEVER −16.2%). MemGen transfers: KodCode → MATH 36.6%→54.2%; GSM8K → science +6.06%, coding +5.1% without degradation elsewhere.
Fig. 4 — Trigger invocation frequency (MemGenSFT+Qwen3-8B, trained on GSM8K). GSM8K avg 86 (+19.6%), GPQA avg 47 (+6.1%), KodCode avg 21 (+3.1%). Invocation rate correlates directly with performance gain. Trigger self-suppresses in unfamiliar domains — structural mechanism behind cross-domain generalisation.
RQ4 — Emergent memory hierarchy (Fig. 6) & trigger ablation
Fig. 6 — Left: performance improves monotonically with K (2→32). Right: selective cluster removal on TriviaQA reveals three distinct memory types with no explicit supervision.
Planning memory
Cluster 2
Task decomposition & step sequencing. Removal → planning failures and compositional reasoning errors spike.
Procedural memory
Cluster 3
Tool usage, formatting, search skills. Removal → tool parse & answer format errors rise.
Working memory
Clusters 1 & 4
Context coherence across session. Removal → think-act inconsistency & task misunderstanding.

Limitations
Review
The paper states the trigger is allowed to fire at any delimiter token — commas and periods — within the generated output. However, every example in Appendix G shows latent tokens appearing only at segment boundaries, before or after think and action tags, never mid-sentence. The paper never explicitly explains this gap. It is not unreasonable to guess that it is a consequence of the reward-adaptive sparsity penalty — the trigger may learn through RL training that mid-sentence invocations don’t improve task reward and get penalized, so it may converge to firing only at semantically meaningful boundaries — but the paper does not confirm this mechanism, so this should be read as a reviewer’s guess, not a claim from the authors.
Limitations
  • ▸Machine-native memory: Latent vectors Mt are human-unreadable — a real limitation. Force-decoding shows only structural artefacts, e.g. Cluster 0 in TriviaQA ends with the pattern “[…]SOC”, Cluster 3 in GSM8K with “[…]_pick”, not human-readable content.
  • ▸Scope: Evaluated only on text-only LLM backbones (Qwen2.5-1.5B, SmolLM3-3B, Qwen3-8B). Extension to multimodal agents is untested.
Summary & conclusion

The authors present MemGen, a dynamic generative latent memory framework that equips any LLM agent with a human-esque cognitive faculty — without modifying the core reasoner πθ.

  • ▸Two trainable LoRA memory components: a memory trigger (trained via RL) decides when to invoke memory; a generative memory weaver (trained via SFT or RL) decides what to reconstruct — producing machine-native latent tokens Mt woven into the hidden-state stream.
  • ▸Consistent gains: MemGen outperforms all 12 baselines across all 9 benchmarks and both backbone sizes, with up to +38.22% over retrieval-based and +13.44% over GRPO methods.
  • ▸Generalisation & continual learning: Training in one domain transfers to unseen domains; catastrophic forgetting is structurally eliminated by isolating experience in θ′ only.
  • ▸Emergent cognition: Without explicit supervision, latent clusters spontaneously specialise into planning, procedural, and working memory — mirroring the structure of human memory systems and suggesting a promising trajectory toward naturalistic machine cognition.
